newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian premier appeals for calm, Yeltsin to speak.
newsitem.headline: Russian premier appeals for calm, Yeltsin to speak.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin appealed to the military to stay calm on Thursday as President Boris Yeltsin considered what to do about accusations that security chief Alexander Lebed was planning a coup d'etat.

But Chernomyrdin, in overall charge of the defence and interior ministries while Yeltsin prepares for heart surgery, rejected Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov's allegation that Lebed was plotting a mutiny.
"I am far from thinking about mutinies and putsches," he told a government meeting.

Yeltsin's press spokesman said the president had not yet decided how to react to the top-level mudslinging, but Itar-Tass news agency quoted spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying he would appear on television at 6 p.m. (1400 GMT).
RIA news agency quoted a Kremlin source as saying the row had "gone too far" and a continuation could threaten Russian security.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, defeated by Yeltsin in the July 3 presidential election, said the argument "could end in a general civil war as well as destroying the army".

The row and the perilous state of the cash-starved Russian military have become intertwined in the war of words between Lebed and Kulikov, who is responsible for the well-equipped interior ministry troops and for the fight against crime.
Lebed is secretary to the influential Security Council and President Boris Yeltsin's personal security adviser.
Lebed, a gruff-voiced former paratroop general, has criticised plans to cut Russia's airborne forces.

Kulikov, a long-standing foe of the security tsar, on Wednesday accused Lebed of planning a "creeping coup" against the authorities in Moscow. Lebed denied the charges and asked Yeltsin for a personal meeting.
The infighting could hardly have come at a worse time for Yeltsin, who is waiting in a sanatorium outside Moscow for doctors to declare him fit enough to undergo heart surgery.

The president, who is holding just a handful of meetings, on Tuesday ordered his Kremlin team to stop squabbling and start working together. But the appeal fell on deaf ears and has been followed by two days of mudslinging.
"The crisis has been mounting for a long time but it broke out rather unexpectedly," wrote Tatyana Malkina, a political observer with the liberal daily newspaper Sevodnya.
"Either Mr Lebed managed simultaneously to annoy a critical number of Russian state officials, or the Kremlin has decided to sack him instead of allowing him to resign proudly."
Lebed, a gravel-voiced reserve paratroop general, joined Yeltsin's team in June after he won 15 percent of the vote in the first round of Russia's presidential election.
He is more popular outside the Kremlin than within it and makes no secret of his presidential ambitions. He could be a magnet for the opposition if he was pushed out now.
Authorities in Moscow and other Russian cities have stepped up security after the allegations by Kulikov, who also said 1,500 Chechen gunmen would help Lebed seize power.
Both Lebed and Chechen rebel commander Aslan Maskhadov denied the allegations.

"We have no intention of getting involved in sorting out sordid squabbles in Moscow," Maskhadov told Radio Russia. "We have enough on our plate. No one has promised anything to anyone and no one will promise anything either."

The political uncertainties unsettled financial markets in Russia and abroad, and Russian share and bond prices both fell. "It's the politics and this Lebed coup business," one London trader of Russian debt said.
